name: Adam Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small company that makes rota and payroll software for care homes, about forty of us in an office above a carpet shop. Most of my day is fixing bugs in the old Java backend, the part that works out night shifts and holiday pay. I like it when a care home manager emails to say the payslips came out right. What wears me out is the stand-up meeting where we pretend a two-day job will take two hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the money side look like for you at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, tight. I'm paid less than most developers I studied with, because there's only my firm and a bank's back office in this town. My partner Lena works nights as a carer at one of the homes that uses our software, and between us we cover the rent and my student loan with maybe three weeks of slack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Honestly, that's the version I'd quietly hope for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, probably a bit too loudly at the pub quiz. I've been saying for two years that the chatbots are a sales pitch, and I'd post something smug about it. Then I'd say the real problem in software was never the code, it was bosses cutting corners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but it doesn't fix my actual problems. I'm still on lower pay in a town with two tech employers, and we've got three weeks of money in the bank. If my firm loses one big care home chain as a client, I'm out of work with nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep refusing the AI code helper our boss keeps pushing on us. I'd ask for a pay rise at my review in March, since I'm doing the same work as people paid more. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside, which sounds tiny but it's what we can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a breath out, mostly. But AI being hype doesn't change the knot in my stomach every time rent day comes round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even the small routine stuff AI does could touch you. Which part of your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing tests and the release notes, mainly. My manager Priyesh already said the AI helper could do the release notes in seconds, and he looked at me when he said it. It's not much of my day, but it's the bit that makes me look busy on the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena say to each other on rent day in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, really. We'd sit at the kitchen table with the banking app open and decide whether the boiler service waits another month. Lena would joke that at least the robots aren't coming for night shifts, and I'd laugh, but not much.

say: I'd say the **AI hype** was always a sales pitch, and I'd say it loudly.
I'd tell people the real problem in software is **bosses cutting corners**, not the code itself.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, but my money problems are exactly the same as before.
Losing **one big client** would put me out of work in a town with two tech employers.
do: Keep refusing the **AI code helper** my boss keeps pushing on the team.
Ask for a **pay rise** at my March review, since I'm paid below others.
Put aside **fifty a month**, which is all the two of us can manage.
feel: Mostly **relief**, with a steady knot of worry every time **rent day** comes round.
S0.quote: AI being hype doesn't change the knot in my stomach every time rent day comes round.
fieldNote: His **rent worries** sit underneath everything; AI hype fading barely touches them.
Says the hype was a con, yet admits the **release notes** task is already eyed by his manager.
Lena's **night shifts** at a client care home tie the household to the same small local economy.

steps.text: Keep fixing payroll bugs by hand without the AI code helper
Ask for a pay rise at the March review
Set up a fifty-a-month standing order into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Coding is on that list, in the middle of the sentence. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's being done to workers, not for them, and I'd keep saying it. At work I'd push our little union branch to ask for a written promise that nobody gets cut because of AI. Online I'd share every story about a firm that sacked half its developers and then had a meltdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be one of the first to go. I'm average, I'm the one who refuses the AI tools, and our boss already counts tickets closed per week. If they need four developers instead of seven, I can tell you which three names are on the list, and mine is one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and get us to ask for a no-redundancy deal before any new AI rollout. I'd probably have to swallow my pride and do the AI helper training the firm offers, even though I hate it. We'd cancel the car lease and Lena would take an extra shift a week, which kills me to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like waiting for a letter you know is coming. I'd be angry at the people selling it and scared at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz, the older guy I eat lunch with. He's fifty-one, he's brilliant at the old payroll rules, and he hates new tools even more than I do. If they cut people, he and I would be standing in the same car park.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You hate the AI helper, but you'd do the training. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't, really, and I know that. It's like joining a protest and then going home and paying the bill anyway. I'd do the training because I can't afford to be the principled one with three weeks of savings.

say: I'd say AI is being **done to workers**, not for them, and that firms are overselling it.
I'd push our **union branch** to demand a written promise of no AI-driven cuts.
think: I'm average and refuse the tools, so I'd be **first on the list** if they cut developers.
With only **three weeks** of savings and few local jobs, losing this job would hit us hard.
do: Push the union branch for a **no-redundancy deal** before any AI rollout.
Sign up, grudgingly, for the firm's **AI helper training** to stay employable.
Cancel the **car lease** while Lena takes one **extra shift** a week.
feel: A sick feeling, like **waiting for a letter** he knows is coming.
**Anger** at the sellers of AI, mixed with plain **fear**.
S1.quote: I can't afford to be the principled one with three weeks of savings.
fieldNote: He openly names himself as **first to be cut**, which makes this alarmed, not just anxious.
His **principles clash** with his bank balance, and he admits the money wins.
Worries for his lunch friend **Tomasz**, which shows his loyalty runs to older colleagues.

steps.text: Push the union branch for a no-redundancy deal before AI rollouts
Sign up for the firm's AI code helper training course
Cancel the car lease and take the bus to work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I don't even know what to say to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, I'd say this is a crisis and the government has to step in, full stop. I'd be at every march about it, and I'd say tech firms should be taxed to pay people while we work out what comes next. I'd stop arguing about whether it's hype, because it wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my job ends within a year of it arriving, maybe sooner. My job is rules, rotas and payroll sums, so the three-year gap before robots is no help to me at all. There's nothing hands-on about what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd stop everything that isn't rent and food and try to save every spare penny, even if it's only a few hundred. Once it arrives I'd sign on for whatever support exists and look for anything hands-on in the care homes, like porter or kitchen work. I genuinely don't have a better plan than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, honestly. I'd be lying awake doing sums that don't add up, and there's no amount of savings I could build in two years that would cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Lena's work is hands-on. Does the robot gap help your household at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps Lena more than me, for maybe three years. She'd be the one earning while I'm not, which flips everything we planned. But care homes would be first in line for robots if they're cheaper than carers on nights, so even her three years feel borrowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the day it's announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably ring my mum, which is pathetic at twenty-seven. Then I'd open the banking app and stare at it. I don't think I'd have a single useful idea that day.

say: I'd call it a **crisis** and say the government must step in straight away.
I'd say tech firms should be **taxed** to pay people while everyone works out what's next.
think: My job is **pure thinking work**, so I'd expect it gone within a year of arrival.
The **robot gap** helps Lena's care job for a while but does nothing for mine.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** only and save every spare penny for two years.
Claim whatever **government support** exists once AGI arrives and the job goes.
Look for **hands-on work** in the care homes, like porter or kitchen jobs.
feel: Plain **panic**, lying awake doing **sums** that don't add up.
S2.quote: My job is rules, rotas and payroll sums, so the three-year gap before robots is no help to me at all.
fieldNote: He has **no real plan** and says so; the thin cushion leaves him no room to make one.
He sees the household **flipping**, with Lena's hands-on care job briefly the only income.
On the day it's announced he'd **ring his mum**, a telling sign of how lost he'd feel.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food only for two years
Claim government support as soon as the payroll job ends
Apply for porter or kitchen jobs at local care homes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but at least it's not tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set the rules, so let's use them. I'd be pushing for a law that makes firms pay into a fund for every job they automate. At work I'd be the annoying one asking management what their plan is for us, every single meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd know I'm still on the wrong side of it, just with a later date. Five years means I'd be thirty-two when the job goes, maybe with a kid by then. That actually scares me more than being twenty-seven with nothing to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd try to get a cheap qualification in something hands-on, maybe an electrician course at the college at night. I'd keep the payroll job as long as it lasts and save harder. Lena and I would probably put off having a baby until we know what's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, like a deadline I didn't agree to. A bit less frantic than the two-year one, but it's still keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an electrician course, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's the bit robots get to last, and someone has to wire the buildings the robots work in. My uncle Pawel did it for thirty years and he's never been out of work. It's also the only course at our college that runs in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the hardest part of putting off a baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Telling Lena's mum, honestly. Lena's thirty in two years and she's always said she wanted kids before thirty-five. Deciding when my partner and I have a baby around a computer's arrival date feels wrong, like the tech firms are picking our family's timing.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to set the rules and should use every one.
I'd push for a law making firms pay into a **fund** for every automated job.
think: I'm still on the **wrong side** of this, just with a later date.
Losing the job at **thirty-two**, maybe with a child, scares me more than losing it now.
do: Take an evening **electrician course** at the town college within two years.
Keep the payroll job as long as possible and **save harder** each month.
Put off **having a baby** with Lena until the picture is clearer.
feel: A **heavy** feeling, like a **deadline** he never agreed to.
S3.quote: Deciding when my partner and I have a baby around a computer's arrival date feels wrong, like the tech firms are picking our family's timing.
fieldNote: Five years makes him **more scared**, not less, because there'd be more at stake by then.
His **electrician** idea comes from his uncle Pawel, a real model he trusts.
Resents tech firms shaping **family timing**, which fits his progressive anger at big firms.

steps.text: Enrol in the evening electrician course at the town college
Campaign for a law making firms fund automated jobs
Raise the monthly savings transfer once the car lease ends
Postpone trying for a baby with Lena for a few years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to do this fairly, if governments actually bother. I'd want free retraining for anyone in a desk job, paid properly, not some online course you do after a twelve-hour shift. And I'd still be at the union meetings, because ten years goes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be all right if I start moving in the next three or four years. The payroll job probably carries on for a while. My worry is that I know myself, and I'll put it off because I hate change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electrician course properly, maybe as an apprenticeship by year three. I'd keep writing software in the meantime because it pays the rent. Lena and I would probably go ahead with the baby, because ten years is too long to put life on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but uneasy underneath. It's the kind of worry you can push to the back of your mind, which is exactly the danger for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd put it off. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years' notice I'd be saying next year, every year, until it's year eight. That's what happened with learning a second programming language, and I'm still only on Java. I'd need Lena to nag me, honestly, and she would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, mostly, if they had a decade and still did nothing. And the big tech firms for taking the money and leaving the mess. But I'd blame myself a bit too, if I had all that time and didn't move.

say: I'd say **a decade** is enough to make this fair, if governments actually try.
I'd demand **paid retraining** for desk workers, not an online course after a long shift.
think: My job probably **carries on** a while, so I'd be fine if I move early.
I know I hate change, so the real risk is that I'll **put it off**.
do: Start an **electrician apprenticeship** by year three while still coding part of the week.
Keep the **software job** to pay rent until the apprenticeship is underway.
Keep going to **union meetings** to push for paid retraining.
feel: Calmer, but with an **uneasy** worry he can push away, which he sees as the **danger**.
S4.quote: With ten years' notice I'd be saying next year, every year, until it's year eight.
fieldNote: The longer time frame mostly worries him because of his own **habit of delay**.
He'd keep **family plans** going here, unlike the five-year picture.
Blames **government** first but accepts some of the blame would be his own.

steps.text: Start an electrician apprenticeship by the third year
Keep coding the payroll software to cover rent meanwhile
Keep going to union meetings about paid retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. With three weeks of savings and two tech employers in town, two years is nothing. What would help is a guaranteed income while people retrain, paid for by the companies making money from it, and a union strong enough to make firms keep their promises.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that nobody asked me if I wanted this. Everyone talks about AI like the weather, but someone is choosing to build it and sell it to my boss. I'd like that person to sit in our stand-up meeting one day.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about AI like the weather, but someone is choosing to build it and sell it to my boss.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old** developer fixing payroll software for care homes in a small town.
He lives with his partner Lena, a **night carer**, with about **three weeks** of savings.
He never uses **AI tools** and admits he'd be first to go if developers were cut.
His mood runs from uneasy in AI Plateau to **panicked** when AGI arrives in two years.
He leans on the **union** and an electrician course, but fears his own habit of delay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years and three weeks of savings leave him no way out.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** during retraining, paid for by the firms profiting from AI.
A **strong union** that can hold employers to their promises.
